---
title: "Estate Planning"
---





## Book Topics

- **Why it matters young**: at 18 your parents lose the right to act for you; set up a plan while you're thinking clearly, since people tend to miss their own cognitive decline
- **Beneficiary designations**: the ten minute task; name a primary and contingent beneficiary on retirement plans, IRAs, HSAs, life insurance, and bank (POD) and brokerage (TOD) accounts; these forms override your will
- **Financial power of attorney**: a durable POA names an agent to handle your money if you can't
- **Healthcare directive and HIPAA release**: a healthcare proxy and living will (often one advance directive), plus a HIPAA form so doctors can share information
- **Will and trust**: a will covers what has no beneficiary, names an executor, and names a guardian for children; without one, state intestate succession decides; most people starting out don't need a trust
- **Paperwork and parents**: store originals safely, keep an account list (no passwords), set up password manager emergency access, and ask your parents about their plan

## What You Own and What You Owe

Your estate starts with your net worth: everything you own minus everything you owe.

**Formula:** Net worth = Total assets − Total debts


::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old](estate_planning_files/figure-html/networth-bar-model-1.png){width=576}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old](estate_planning_files/figure-html/networth-bar-model-2.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $8,000 + $9,000) − ($6,000 + $1,000) = $35,000 − $7,000 = a net worth of $28,000.

::: panel-tabset
## Excel

Assuming assets are listed in `B2:B5` and debts in `C2:C3`:

```swift
=SUM(B2:B5) - SUM(C2:C3)
```

## Python

`net_worth()` takes two dictionaries, so you can see each item and the total.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def net_worth(assets, debts):
    return sum(assets.values()) - sum(debts.values())

assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
debts = {"car_loan": 6000, "credit_card": 1000}
print(net_worth(assets, debts))
#> 28000
```
:::


Sanity check: paying off the credit card from savings doesn't change net worth.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
assets_after = {**assets, "savings": 8000 - 1000}
debts_after = {**debts, "credit_card": 0}
print(net_worth(assets_after, debts_after))
#> 28000
```
:::


Edge case: net worth can be negative.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(net_worth({"savings": 3000, "car": 5000}, {"student_loans": 30000}))
#> -22000
```
:::


## R

`net_worth()` takes two named vectors, so you can see each item and the total.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
net_worth <- function(assets, debts) {
  sum(assets) - sum(debts)
}

assets <- c(k401 = 12000, roth_ira = 6000, savings = 8000, car = 9000)
debts  <- c(car_loan = 6000, credit_card = 1000)
net_worth(assets, debts)
#> [1] 28000
```
:::


Sanity check: paying off the credit card from savings doesn't change net worth. Cash goes down by $1,000 and so does debt.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
assets_after <- replace(assets, "savings", 8000 - 1000)
debts_after  <- replace(debts, "credit_card", 0)
net_worth(assets_after, debts_after)
#> [1] 28000
```
:::


Edge case: net worth can be negative. A recent graduate with $3,000 in savings, a $5,000 car, and $30,000 in student loans starts below zero, and that's common.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
net_worth(assets = c(savings = 3000, car = 5000),
          debts  = c(student_loans = 30000))
#> [1] -22000
```
:::


:::

How to read this result: net worth is the yearly check in on your progress. It's also roughly what your estate would be worth today, before adding any life insurance.

## How Much Your Beneficiary Forms Control

Life insurance isn't part of net worth while you're alive, but it pays out when you die. Add it, then split the estate by what decides who gets each piece.

**Formula:** Share controlled by beneficiary forms = Assets with a named beneficiary ÷ Total estate


::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![What decides who gets each part of the estate](estate_planning_files/figure-html/beneficiary-bar-model-1.png){width=576}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![What decides who gets each part of the estate](estate_planning_files/figure-html/beneficiary-bar-model-2.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $45,000 + $8,000) ÷ $80,000 = about 89% of the estate, decided by forms that take minutes to fill out. That's why beneficiary designations come before a will for most young people.

::: panel-tabset
## Excel

Assuming assets with a named beneficiary are in `B2:B5` and assets without one are in `C2`:

```swift
=SUM(B2:B5) / (SUM(B2:B5) + SUM(C2))
```

To test blank forms, list every asset in `B2:B6` with `Yes` or `No` in `C2:C6` for "has a beneficiary," then:

```swift
=SUMIF(C2:C6, "Yes", B2:B6) / SUM(B2:B6)
```

## Python

`beneficiary_share()` divides what the forms control by the whole estate.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary):
    named = sum(with_beneficiary.values())
    return named / (named + sum(without_beneficiary.values()))

with_beneficiary = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "life_insurance": 45000, "savings_pod": 8000}
without_beneficiary = {"car": 9000}
print(beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary))
#> 0.8875
```
:::


What if some forms are blank?


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
all_assets = {"401k": 12000, "roth_ira": 6000, "life_insurance": 45000,
              "savings": 8000, "car": 9000}
scenarios = {
    "all forms filled": ["401k", "roth_ira", "life_insurance", "savings"],
    "no POD on savings": ["401k", "roth_ira", "life_insurance"],
    "only the 401(k)": ["401k"],
    "no forms at all": [],
}
for name, named in scenarios.items():
    yes = {k: v for k, v in all_assets.items() if k in named}
    no = {k: v for k, v in all_assets.items() if k not in named}
    print(f"{name:<18} {beneficiary_share(yes, no):>5.0%}  through will: ${sum(no.values()):,}")
#> all forms filled     89%  through will: $9,000
#> no POD on savings    79%  through will: $17,000
#> only the 401(k)      15%  through will: $68,000
#> no forms at all       0%  through will: $80,000
```
:::


## R

`beneficiary_share()` divides what the forms control by the whole estate.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
beneficiary_share <- function(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary) {
  sum(with_beneficiary) / (sum(with_beneficiary) + sum(without_beneficiary))
}

with_beneficiary    <- c(k401 = 12000, roth_ira = 6000, life_insurance = 45000, savings_pod = 8000)
without_beneficiary <- c(car = 9000)
beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary)
#> [1] 0.8875
```
:::


What if some forms are blank? A blank form moves that account into the "will or state law" pile. Each scenario below starts from the same $80,000 estate.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
all_assets <- c(k401 = 12000, roth_ira = 6000, life_insurance = 45000,
                savings = 8000, car = 9000)
scenarios <- list(
  "all forms filled"   = c("k401", "roth_ira", "life_insurance", "savings"),
  "no POD on savings"  = c("k401", "roth_ira", "life_insurance"),
  "only the 401(k)"    = c("k401"),
  "no forms at all"    = character(0)
)
data.frame(
  scenario     = names(scenarios),
  forms_share  = sapply(scenarios, function(s)
    beneficiary_share(all_assets[s], all_assets[!names(all_assets) %in% s])),
  through_will = sapply(scenarios, function(s) sum(all_assets[!names(all_assets) %in% s])),
  row.names    = NULL
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   scenario          forms_share through_will
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 all forms filled        0.888         9000
#> 2 no POD on savings       0.788        17000
#> 3 only the 401(k)         0.15         68000
#> 4 no forms at all         0            80000
```
:::


:::

How to read this result: the higher the share, the less your will has to do. With every form filled in, a will only decides the car. With no forms, all $80,000 goes through probate.
